speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the intention, of the government to proceed with the various bills on the order paper before taking up further estimates. The house resumed from Friday, June 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 81, to amend the Dominion Franchise Act (dominion by-elections)'-Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Sanderson in the chair).
On section 2-Qualifications.

Mr. Chairman, when we
dealt with this bill the other day the leader of the opposition suggested that we let stand subparagraph (c) of paragraph (B) of section 2, which deals with the qualifications of the voter, and in the last lines of which appear the words "and has continued to be ordinarily resident therein until polling day." The right hon, gentleman very properly pointed out that this condition could not be foreseen. Evidently the intention was to cover the case of the rural voter who can always present himself at the poll at the last moment, but that case is already covered by the Dominion Elections Act. There seems to be no purpose in having this provision here, and I would ask the chairman of the special committee to move to strike out those words.

I move:

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of bill No. 83, to amend the Judges Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Salaries of judges of Supreme Court of Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I informed the minister when we were discussing the resolution in committee that I thought, as I still do, that the necessity for increasing the personnel of the high court in Ontario would disappear if those who had attained a condition which rendered it impossible for them to discharge their duties as they should were to resign their positions. I hold that opinion very strongly. I trust that the reports which have appeared in the newspapers as to the purpose of this legislation are not accurate and that there is some real necessity for this bill beyond political needs. After carefully considering the matter, I do not think it would serve any useful purpose to go through the various provinces and name those whom it is quite apparent should retire.
I would point out that we endeavoured to meet the situation some years ago by offering a bill to the house providing for retirement at seventy-five years. However, the Senate thought it undesirable that a change should be made without conditions, and the bill did not pass. The Minister of Justice of to-day took the view that some provision should be made to safeguard the interests of those who were affected by the legislation, to which my answer then was, and now is, that there is an implied condition in the appointment of a man to the bench that he shall be reasonably efficient for the purposes for which he is appointed, and if through physical or mental disability he is unable to discharge those duties, he has forfeited his position and should resign. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is responsible for the provision that ultimately found its place in the statute books. For the reasons which he gave the other day, and which I believe are cogent reasons, it is very undesirable to have a commission appointed to inquire into the physical or mental condition of those who hold judicial office. Such a procedure would be calculated to drag the judiciary into a certain measure of contempt. Having regard to what I consider to be the larger phase of the question, namely, the public interest, I shall refrain from making any criticism beyond saying that I do feel it is almost an intolerable condition in a country such as this that there should be men willing to accept positions on the implied condition that they will be able to continue to discharge their duties and who, despite the fact that they are not-even on their own
Judges Act Amendment

admission-continue to hold office and draw the emoluments of their positions. I shall be much censured for making these observations by those who belong to that favoured class, the judiciary, but that is not going to deter me in any sense from discharging what I conceive to be my duty.
Had it not been that the bill to which I referred was destroyed in the Senate, the necessary arrangements would have been made and it would have been unnecessary to appoint these two judges. If every man was functioning according to the implied condition of his appointment, it would be wholly unnecessary that there should be any additions made to this court. There will be incurred an annual expense of $18,000, in addition to travelling expenses, which need not be incurred were the duties of office discharged to the extent to which I believe there is an implied undertaking that they should be.
I repeat that I make these observations with some reluctance. I believe that the larger public interest should induce me to refrain from going into details. I indicated the other day that. I would give much thought to this matter. I have, and I have concluded that the larger public interest is more important than the interest of the individuals in question. There would appear to be a seeming unwillingness on the part of these men to realize their obligations to the public in the same way as they compel litigants appearing before them to recognize their obligations. If an action were brought by a trained and skilled man to recover his salary, if it could be proven that he was in either the physical or the mental condition of some members of the courts, he could not recover, and it would be the duty of those who now continue to hold office to decide that he could not recover on the ground that he had not fulfilled that condition of special knowledge and fitness which is the very essence of the appointment. That is all I have to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With
some, even most, of the points raised by my right hon. friend when this matter was before the committee on the resolution that preceded the bill, and with what he has just said, I agree. But I think the question presents itself to us in this simple way. The legislature of Ontario, in the exercise of its undoubted jurisdiction, and for reasons which I think are valid, has increased by two the number of judges in. the high court, trial division, of that province. Are there any reasons for our refusing to implement the wish of the province in the matter, even if some of us think that possibly, by some other arrangement with regard to the superannuation of old

judges or in some other way, these two additional judges might be done without? Can we tell the province of Ontario that we refuse to implement their legislation, which. they have the right to pass, because we have not yet made up our minds os to what we ought to do with respect to judges who have reached old age or are afflicted with some physical infirmity that prevents them from doing all that they could do on the bench previously?
In the first place, what the province says is that it wants two additional judges for the trial division. I do not think the condition my right hon. friend mentions applies to the trial division of Ontario, according to information given me by members of parliament who are practising law in that province. There are at the present time eleven judges in the trial division. As I said on the resolution, two of them cannot work very well on the ordinary business of the court for the reason that one of them is working continuously on the board under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, devoting all his time thereto, while the other is engaged entirely on bankruptcy matters demanding the whole of -his time. Then we have increased the work of the judges in Ontario. Two years ago we increased it by handing over to them the adjudication of matrimonial cases and I understand that, notwithstanding what was said here at the time-that this new method would result in a diminution of divorces- divorce cases have as a matter of fact vastly increased since this law was passed, and a great part of the time of the judges is taken up with these cases.
Now that the attorney general of Ontario has given 'his reasons to the legislature, which they find to be valid, may I repeat, just for the purpose of giving information to the committee, certain facts with respect to the courts.
There are forty-seven county and district towns-that is, outside the city of Toronto- where at least two courts a year and in many cases four are held. In the majority of cases the duration of the court is about one week. In Sandwich, Hamilton, London and Ottawa the jury- courts, of which there are two each year, usually last for at least three weeks and the non-jury courts, of which there are two each year, also usually last for at least two weeks. In some of the other county and district towns to which a judge is assigned for one week it often happens that a longer period than a week is required to dispose of the cases that are ready for trial. A weekly court is also held at London and Ottawa on Saturday morning, and this necessitates a judge going to each of these cities every Saturday.

Judges Act Amendment
In the city of Toronto a jury court sits three times each year and is usually engaged about eight weeks. At each of such sittings it usually happens that some of the civil cases are not dealt with and it is necessary that they stand over until the next court. The non-jury court at Toronto is a continuous court and sits the year round except for the period of court vacation. In this court the work is particularly heavy and in an effort to reduce the list to a size which will permit the hearing of cases within a reasonable time after they have been set down, it has been necessary for some years now to have two courts sitting. The Toronto weekly court, in which most of the time of the court is devoted to the hearing of motions, sits continuously the year round except- for the court vacation periods, and the court usually lasts the better part of a day, five days a week. Then the questions of bankruptcy and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act are dealt w-ith.
I believe that the duty of this parliament and my duty as Minister of Justice is to see that the administration of justice in Ontario should be carried out reasonably, and those who have the responsibility there are those who know whether or not we should proceed in the way provided for in this bill. As to the other question, which arises incidentally- and I know my right hon. friend has this in mind-there is in two or three provinces more than room for improvement in view of the conditions that exist there. But as my right hon. friend knows, I have given this matter a good deal of attention, and I am inclined to agree with the members of the Canadian Bar Association, who have been specially charged with the investigation of this matter and who recommend that we should revert to the condition that existed before the amendment of 1920 and permit judges who have reached the age of seventy-five and who have been for a stated number of years on the bench-twenty years-to retire with the salary which they received on the bench. This was changed in 1920. The committee of the Canadian Bar Association favour this change. They suggest that we might require judges who have retired under such a provision to serve in emergency casies, or when there is need of their services, at the request of the chief justice of their court, and that they should retain their rank in the judiciary.
There is much to commend this to the favourable consideration of parliament. I have said that I am inclined to favour it. I submitted the matter to my colleagues, and, while I do not want to betray any secrets, . I may say they thought that this is no time for increases of pensions or things of that kind, and in my private conversations with
my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) I learn he also thinks that this would have no chance of getting through parliament at the present time. Possibly that is so. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Ca'han) not only suggested but almost sought to impose upon us the necessity of adopting the drastic method he advised; he accused all the ministers of justice of lack of moral courage in not having taken advantage of a provision in the statute under which, if it is believed that a judge is not physically fit to do his work, an investigation may be held, a regular trial at which witnesses may be heard, and on a report being made accordingly, the judge in question would cease to receive any salary. I do not think this would increase the dignity of the bench and enhance respect for the courts.
When my hon. frie-nd said that it was while I was Minister of Justice that this provision was put on the statutes, I did not remember it, and I investigated the matter. I found that it was done in 1922 when Sir Lomer Gouin was Minister of Justice, and he was responsible for it in a peculiar way. There had been amendments to the Judges Acts, and when they were being discussed by the other house it was Senator Barnard who moved that amendment, and he was supported by members of that house who were strong opponents of the government. At the time, as my hon. friend knows, the party which now sits on this side of the house was in power, but very little so in the senate, as is the case at the present time. However, when the amendment came back to the house the then Minister of Justice merely said that he had no objection to it. That hardly supports the view of my hon. friend that this is my work, or even that of the government of the time.

I was not pressing that
point. I was just trying to recollect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
However, that has never been applied up to the present time. Of course in the provisions of the law affecting county court judges there is a stipulation of this kind, although not so drastic, of which advantage has been taken. I myself recommended a few years ago an investigation in Manitoba, but I must say that before I did it I had received an application from the bar association of that province, and it was because complaints were officially placed before the Department of Justice that this extraordinary method was adopted. I think I may say that if either the Canadian Bar Association or the bar association of any province-because they know the facts better

Judges Act Amendment

than anybody else-would officially ask for action as provided for in the section mentioned by my hon. friend, I woidd deem it my duty to take the necessary proceedings. But as it is, could the Minister of Justice act proprio motu or merely because he hears rumours and because certain newspapers have published some reports? It would be a very dangerous thing to do, and if the judge concerned had been in years gone by an opponent of the party in power, possibly the minister would be accused of having his actions dictated by political considerations. We must leave the bench absolutely outside of any possible suspicions about politics, and especially so with regard to any action that could be taken by the Department of Justice with regard to judges. A law could be made, as it applies to the Supreme Court of Canada and the federal courts, so that when a judge reaches a certain age he has to leave the bench. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George objects to age being taken into consideration. He says that in some cases old men are better than young men. I agree with him-

I was objecting to age
being the sole consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -but I think the exceptions confirm the rule and that is being done in other countries. My right hon. friend was right when he said the other day that seventy-two years had been recommended as the age limit by the commissioners in England who considered that question. As a matter of fact at the present time county court judges are retired at seventy-two years of age, but there is a provision that if the Justice department considers their services could still be utilized, their term of office may be prolonged from year to year. I do not approve of the department intervening in the matter; I think retirement should be provided for without the executive having anything to do with making the decision. However, all that will have to be considered and will have to be dealt with. I do not like the drastic section of the Judges Act which was placed in the statutes in 1922 and which has never been acted upon. But we must do something to prevent possible abuses, and if my right hon. friend is correct-and I think he is-there are certain abuses. I submit, however, that this is only incidental to the present bill; we are merely asked to give effect to the statutes of Ontario, and they have the right to ask us so to do.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was entirely right in saying he was not the author of the provision in the statute of 1922. If anything I said would

indicate that he was, I knew better, because I took the trouble to follow it up. It was introduced in the other chamber, as he suggested, and it came to this chamber and was accepted by the Commons. The present Minister of Justice was then, if I remember, Minister of Marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I was a sailor at the time.

Well, he has been in stormy seas since. This statute, being a statute of the province of Ontario, is being acted upon with greater celerity than usual. It was late in April when the statute increasing the bench by two was passed, and during my short time in parliament I have seen a year or more go by without any action being taken by the federal authority to implement an increase, for economic or other reasons. I remember one occasion when no provision was made for quite a considerable time, on the theory that there was really no necessity for the increase. I had thought that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act ' would not be permanent and would not engage a judge's entire working hours for very long. In respect to bankruptcy, the registrar really does most of the work, but the judge must take certain steps because he does the final act.
I quite agree also that the discussion with respect to the tenure of office is but incidental to this question. I brought it up because there might be no other opportunity except on the estimates to refer to it, and I thought it well to refer to it. The answer I make to my hon. friend, and I am sure he had had it in mind-it was in the mind of those with whom I have discussed it-is that to provide at this time that all judges of a certain age should receive full pay would have the effect at once of inducing all those who had been superannuated and had attained that age to demand equal treatment, and I have not seen any answer that I could reasonably make to that request. I did look into the matter very carefully during the time we were in office, and I gathered from discussions that I had in various parts of the country that there was a general feeling that to undertake to increase pensions of the judiciary at this time would be an impolitic thing to do. I should be sorry if my hon. friend should conclude that I suggested he could not put the amendment to the Judges Act through if he so desired, for his majority is ample for that purpose. What I did mean to convey was that I do not think it carries the general approval of the country or of parliament, for reasons that I need not discuss. The very

Judges Act Amendment
suggestion of members of the judiciary holding on and continuing in office when they must know of their own limitations is an effort to induce parliament to do something under duress, if I may use that word-wrongly in that sense, perhaps-but under compulsion or of necessity. To be compelled by that method to provide pensions would not be a nice thing for this parliament, and would be resented I think by many people in every part of the country.
I was not able to look up the royal commission which investigated the matter in England; I am glad the hon. gentleman has done so, because my memory was that the age of retirement recommended was seventy-two or seventy-three, I was not sure which.
I should like to refer briefly to one point to which the minister directed attention, namely the ability to utilize the services of those who have retired but who are in good health. In England a retired judge frequently goes down at Christmas to help out in the divorce, admiralty and probate divisions. The late Lord Mersey used to do it frequently, helping the courts to dispose of arrears before the Christmas vacation. But in this country where you have the double jurisdiction there is that difficulty. The dominion would have to provide that they should be paid no salary beyond their retiring allowance. Clearly the province could not confer jurisdiction upon a retired judge to act, and clearly we would have to amend our statute to provide for it. There are grave complications. The matter was looked into once by a minister of justice and by one of the officials of the Department of Justice, and no conclusion was arrived at. I favour the proposal, and if the minister could work out any plan by which retired judges might be enabled to render service as judges through cooperative action on the part of the provinces and the dominion, I think it would be very desirable and would serve a useful purpose, permitting the attorneys general, with the aid perhaps of the Minister of Justice, to call upon a retired judge in times of stress to render further service without the payment of any further compensation than travelling expenses. Certainly in England where they have the unitary system, it is feasible, but under the complex system of the provinces determining the number of judges and the dominion providing their salaries it might require joint legislative action.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no doubt about it.
Can the Minister of Justice give the committee information as to the number of judges in each province who are appointed by the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In Ontario in the high court there will be, when this bill becomes law and is acted upon, twenty-one judges. In Nova Scotia there are 8-chief justice, judge in equity, judge in divorce, and 5 puisne judges. In New Brunswick there are 8 judges of the high court.
The judge in divorce is also a judge in the same manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I include him. In Manitoba there are 11 judges; in British Columbia, 11; in Saskatchewan. 12; in Alberta, 11 judges of the high court. There are 3 in Prince Edward Island, and there is one in the Yukon territory. I will come to Quebec in a moment.
In addition to these there are the county court judges, who are also appointed by the federal government. In Ontario there are authorized-I do not say they are all appointed, but almost all-75 judges of the county and district courts. In Nova Scotia there are 7 county court judges; in New Brunswick, 6; in Manitoba, 9 and one junior county court judge. In British Columbia there are 14 judges and junior judges; in Prince Edward Island there are 3. In Saskatchewan there are 18 district court judges, and in Alberta, 12.
In Quebec the high court judges do most of the work that is assigned to the county court judges; there are no county court judges in Quebec. There are 12 judges of the court of king's bench as the appeal court, and there are 37 judges of the superior court. There are no other judges appointed in the province of Quebec by the federal government.

Is there not a smaller
court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I should mention the circuit court of the district of Montreal.
Which is similar to the county court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; there are 4 judges, consisting of a senior judge and three other judges. The senior judge is paid $8,000 per annum and the three others are paid $7,000 per annum. Those judges are sitting in addition to the high court judges of the province of Quebec.
Is it a fact that there are only forty-nine judges appointed by the federal government in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; there are magistrates appointed by the provincial government.

How is there such a wide discrepancy between Quebec and Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because the systems are altogether different. In Quebec there are no county court judges, while Ontario has a large number of them. But as the hon. member will have noticed, there are. less high court judges in Ontario than in Quebec. There are only twenty-one high court judges in Ontario and there are thirty-seven in the trial division of the superior court in Quebec, plus twelve appeal court judges.

As a layman the fact which appeals to me is that in Ontario there are ninety-six judges while in Quebec there are only forty-nine. I assume those forty-nine judges must be doing the same work as the ninety-six in Ontario.
' Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East): Except that in Quebec judges are appointed by the province to deal with smaller cases which are considered by county court judges in' Ontario. Secondly, I do not believe there is a very great discrepancy in the matter of expense, because the high court judges are paid $9,000 and the county court judges $5,000.
What is the expense per capita as compared to Great Britain?

Dairy Industry Act

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 56, to amend the Dairy Industry Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Sale of butter.
The minister might explain the general purpose of the clause and just why this change is being made.

Section 1 amends subsection 3 of section 6 of the Dairy Industry Act. Subsection 3 of section 6 of the act reads:
No person shall sell, offer or have in his possession for sale,
(a) any butter moulded or cut into prints, blocks, squares or pats ...
That subsection is repealed, and the subclause that is being substituted for it by this bill makes this change only, that instead of confining the size of prints to quarter pounds, half pounds, one pound and two pounds, it makes it possible to have them in any multiple of a pound. The chief reason for the change is that it is customary in British Columbia and in other places to sell butter in three pound prints, and under the present law that is not legal.
There is a line underlined at the end of paragraph (a). Is that new?

That is just a rewording of the language of the old act. The words in the old act were "as sold by farmers" and the amending words are "manufactured by individual farmers and sold by them." The butter must be made by the farmers as well as sold by them.
Were any representations made by the dairy council or other agricultural interests asking for these amendments?

Representations were
made. I am not sure whether by the dairy council or not, asking for these amendments, and the department considered them in the interests of the dairy industry, particularly in British Columbia.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Cheese.
What is the reason for this change?

The reason for this has to do with the recommendations that were made by the price spreads commission last year. One of their suggestions, which has been discussed at some length, was to the
effect that we should have prints of cheese made in multiples of a pound rather than in sizes of, say, five ounces, six and a half ounces or seven and a half ounces. This amendment provides that the prints must be put up in either multiples of a pound or in divisions of a pound, such as a quarter of a pound, or half a pound. It is one of the suggestions that was made in connection with the inquiry by the price spreads commission of the sizes of packages offered to the public for sale.
But the individual farmer may sell cheese in any way he likes?

A phrase similar to the one used at the end of the previous subsection is contained here, "but nothing in this subsection shall be held to apply to cheese of indiscriminate weight manufactured by individual farmers and sold by them." That is, home-made cheese is not subject to this legislation.
Wrhat is the meaning of "indiscriminate" weight?
It can be any weight at all; it is not confined to multiples or divisions of a pound, if made and sold by a farmer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Marine) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the constitution of a corporation to be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of carrying on a national broadcasting service in Canada in the place and stead of the present Canadian radio broadcasting commission, to provide for honorariums, remuneration, salaries and other expenses incidental thereto, to authorize the governor in council to make certain advances for purposes therein mentioned, and to repeal the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are
some features of the report made by the special committee that dealt with the radio question to which I should like to direct attention. The report was a unanimous one. It contemplates the creation of a corporation similar to the British Broadcasting Corporation. I do not think the committee realized
Broadcasting Corporation

the difference between conditions in Great Britain and here. In the first phase of its report the committee recommend:
That in the opinion of your committee radio broadcasting could be best conducted by a general manager.
In 1934 the radio committee made the same recommendation; there is nothing new about that. That is the experience of Great Britain, where they are carrying on their broadcasting through a corporation with a general manager. He is a very eminent man, a scholar, an Oxford man possessing wide administrative experience. In this country he would be regarded as an extremely high type of official. He was drawn from the great reservoir that they have in Great Britain from which to draw men of this type for public service, and he has rendered conspicuous service to his country in the position which he holds. But when you come to appoint a general manager in Canada you find many difficulties in the way. I am not going to do more than point out that as far back as 1934 certain recommendations were made but were not acted upon because we realized, after the closest inquiry, that you cannot say that because a given condition in Great Britain assures certain results, different conditions in Canada will make the same results possible.
The report of the committee contemplates a condition exactly opposite to that which prevails in Great Britain. There are no such things as private broadcasting stations in Great Britain; all the broadcasting stations are under the sole control of the corporation, of which Sir John Reith is general manager. Owing to lack of funds, our organization was not able to build stations. It had to utilize, by leases and other arrangements, the existing facilities for the purpose of carrying out its undertaking. There was a constant endeavour on the part of private interests to secure licences for new stations. Under the existing law, the responsibility of deciding whether or not a new station shall be licensed rests with the commission and its technical officers; under the conditions that the committee reports upon, it will be left to someone in the Department of Transport, now the Department of Marine. I may say to the minister at once that that means disaster to the broadcasting undertaking in this country.
We know

it is not merely guessing-that very large numbers of people are constantly seeking licences for broadcasting stations. If the political department-I use the word in its broad sense-is to deal with these applications, an inevitable result will follow. Hon. members of this committee must know that

applications were refused by the commission, because part of the basis of the complaints against the commission was that it would not continue to grant licences. All you have to do is grant enough licences and you destroy the public character of Canadian broadcasting. At the moment we have secured the ownership of this facility, or utility, or whatever you may call it, in the people of Canada, and we have ensured it against destruction by private interests, but the private interests have been very vigilant. They have been watchful of their own interests and have determined that if it is within their power, this facility is not to function as a public enterprise. They have determined fairly and legitimately, so far as that is concerned, to destroy this publicly owned facility. Their idea is that it should be in the hands of private enterprise. The two or three great enterprises across the line have watched with increasing anxiety the operations of this publicly owned facility. They do not desire that their privately owned enterprises should be regarded merely as tentative experiments; they wish to continue as a privately owned enterprise and not be merged in a publicly owned and controlled broadcasting system such as we have in this country.
I point this out because if broadcasting in Canada is to be in the hands of a corporation, and that is what the report of the committee recommends, then you will have to ensure its continuance and life. If a department of government is to determine whether or not additional licences shall be issued for private stations, I say again that will mean the end of our publicly owned radio broadcasting facilities. If the minister will look into the matter under present conditions, he will have no difficulty in realizing why I say this.
One step further. When the former government brought this broadcasting enterprise into being as a publicly owned facility, it had first of all to take up with the United States the question of channels. This was an international side of the matter which had to be considered, and -there were many difficulties that had to be dealt with. They were fairly successfully overcome, but private interests were constantly demanding that their facilities should be used. The existing channels were in the hands of private interests in all parts of -the country, except possibly in British Columbia which was not adequately covered. The newspapers had facilities of their own, private interests had facilities of their own, and the result was that the commission, being without adequate funds, was compelled to

Broadcasting Corporation
make the best arrangements possible for the purpose of carrying on to the extent of its ability in broadcasting throughout the dominion.
I do not agree with the general tenor of the report of the committee with regard to the operations of the commission. It is human because it is composed of individuals. It 'had to meet an extraordinary situation. Without money, and limited to the revenues from licences, it had to provide coverage from Great Britain to Vancouver. Notwithstanding the terms in which the report of the special committee refers to the result of its efforts, in countries other than Canada this experiment has been regarded as very successful utider the circumstances. It is not encouraging to those who devoted their time to this matter, who laboured as they did and brought about results which were noted very highly in other countries, to find a committee of the House of Commons investigating their efforts and speaking of them in the terms in which they did. Undoubtedly mistakes were made, but I do not think anyone can deny that mistakes would be made in the bringing into being of a commission such as this. The commission was faced with difficulties in connection with complaints as to interference. There was a clashing in channels and there was also interference from the large powerful stations across the line.
The programs that were put upon the air reflected some measure of credit upon the Canadian enterprise. We could not expect that 11,000,000 people would be able to provide facilities comparable to those at the disposition of the two or three great private enterprises in the United States. Having made the election that we did, that is, to create a publicly owned enterprise, we would be manifestly unfair to attach too much criticism to the fact that in the judgment of some it does not compare favourably with the high powered stations in another country built up at the cost of millions of dollars. The temptation merely to copy slavishly the method adopted in another country for the purpose of operating this facility is very great, and the minister will find that conditions are quite different both as to ownership of facilities and as to the attitude of mind of the public to the facility, to advertising and advertisers and to the general situation. For instance, it is well known that facilities have been established in countries across the channel for the purpose of advertising in Great Britain and Ireland. That is well known. We have had many problems in connection with advertising. We have had very acute problems in connection with the language used on the radio-complaints from western Canada on the one hand, and on the other complaints from eastern Canada-and the endeavour to navigate through a very difficult channel and through very stormy waters the ship that was launched under such conditions *has not been an easy task.
I can only say to the minister, without going into the matter in further detail, that if the question of licences is to be determined by a political body, namely, the government or any department of government rather than by the corporation itself, then the corporation is destined to be supplanted in its public operations by private enterprises, because in the very nature of things we have not provided the money to carry on the kind of organization one would like to carry on. We increased the licence fee to two dollars, with much complaint and criticism, in order that the commission might have larger funds at its disposal. In its report the committee suggests that the government may lend money to the commission for the purpose of enabling it to provide facilities. The minister knows what difficulties will be encountered there. It is better to provide in the estimates for a loan to them so that they will be free as a corporation to spend it, than to leave them in a position where they will have to make application for the purpose of securing loans; for then there will enter into the question the many factors that have brought disaster to many of our enterprises of a public character, and it will certainly not enure to the henefit of this institution if we are to maintain it as it now is, a publicly owned facility operating for the people at no cost at the present time except the licence fee of two dollars. No country in the world that I know of, except some smaller European countries, is placed in a more difficult position than ourselves. You have great and powerful stations in New York, in Cincinnati and on the Pacific slope; and when the words have been projected into the air- they no longer say the ether-when they have been projected into space they go north as well as south, and you tune in your radio and hear what is being said. There is no way of controlling it adequately, and that is why some people have unfavourably compared our operations with those of the great republic. The multiplication of privately owned stations under any circumstances will be detrimental to the interests of this publicly owned facility, whether it be held and operated by the commission or by a corporation; and the essential limitation that has been imposed upon this undertaking by reason of our geographical position and lack of means has not made it
Broadcasting Corporation

possible to carry on in the way in which one would have liked. But I should like my fellow Canadians to think that the opinions expressed in other parts of the world as to what we have been able to do reflect credit at least upon Canada and Canadians and do not deserve unrestrained criticism, as will be found in some parts of the report to which I refer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext:
Radio broadcasting in Canada has been studied by one royal commission and three parliamentary committees, and these four reports agree on the broad principles that must govern us. That is to say, the aim of broadcasting should be a complete coverage by government facilities and the present situation demands complete control over all forms of broadcasting whether public or private. These conditions are being maintained in the present bill. There is no question whatsoever as to whether this bill is the last word m radio broadcasting. The government believes, however, having in mind the reports of these various committees, that the bill does represent the consensus of opinion as to the next step to be taken. We know that many conditions affecting radio broadcasting at the present time are unsatisfactory. I assume that more mail comes into my office protesting against various phases of broadcasting than against any other matter with which my department has to deal. Many of these complaints are frivolous; nevertheless the volume and general character indicate that there is something lacking in the present situation.
This bill follows very closely the report of the committee, and I believe that had the earlier legislation conformed more nearly to the reports of the royal commission and of the parliamentary committee that preceded the introduction of that legislation, perhaps we should not have wandered afield in our attempt to reach the ultimate goal. My right hon. friend has mentioned the fact that this gives power to the minister to licence private broadcasting stations. The minister has that power to-day; it is inherent in the Radiotelegraph Act of Canada.

The only action I have taken in that regard is to refuse recommendations of the commission in the direction of issuing two additional broadcasting licences.

We have in Canada, as those familiar with radio matters agree, far too many private licences to-day for stations of small power, and the result is that the channels of communication are becoming very much involved. It is almost impossible to find a clear channel for a station of high power such as is needed to hold our place against the high powered stations across the line and particularly in Mexico, and in my opinion very serious consideration must be given to straightening out the situation that has been caused by the granting of so many licences to small powered stations. That is one of the most serious problems to be considered.

speechtext: I cannot say what was contemplated, but my observation leads me to believe that very little was done; in fact, the situation has become worse. That is my personal opinion, based on what I have seen since I took over control of the department which is responsible for this matter. I think the control of broadcasting is inherent in the government everywhere. Even in Great Britain the British Broadcasting Corporation does not determine the allocation of channels.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext: It is a monopoly.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext:
Of course they have a
monopoly; nevertheless the power to allocate channels is vested in the Post Office Department under their radiotelegraph act. Similarly in the United States the power is vested in the government through an act of congress. This is logically a function of government in that the-channels are arranged by government negotiations. It will be remembered that all the governments interested in telegraphs met at Madrid some few years ago and worked out the allocation of free channels between the various countries. I think there is no particular occasion for criticism, but this can be discussed when the clauses are before us in committee, and I assure my right hon. friend that the government is not committed to the exact method set out in the bill; it is quite willing to consider modifications. All I wish to point out is that the government has always had that power and has always exercised it, but under the last act it was bound to receive, if not to accept, the recommendation of the commission.
I do not know that anything further need be said at this time. The bill can be more effectively discussed when it is before us. I think everyone in Canada realizes the difficulty of the situation. The very limited funds at the disposal of the commission are a great restriction. We collect and turn over to the

Broadcasting Corporation
commission roughly about a million and a half dollars a year. In Great Britain about ten times that amount is collected; in Australia also, a country with a smaller population than Canada, the amount is larger. It seems to me fairly well fixed in everyone's mind that a fee of two dollars is about all that can be expected.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext: All the traffic will bear. That of course is one great limitation. Then we have the tremendous cost of wire charges to cover the country from coast to coast. Further, we have a situation which is perhaps peculiar to this country, arising from the competition of high powered stations to the south of us broadcasting expensive programs which naturally invite comparison with ours. Considering the amount of the expenditure for programs, I think we have very little to be ashamed of at the moment. My feeling is that we have done extraordinarily well with the funds that have been made available. But I have not the slightest doubt that the committee have reported a program which should be adopted in Canada. As we know, the former act has not been satisfactory; it has been amended from time to time to permit it to operate. There are some features that are quite unworkable without amending legislation, and I sincerely commend the bill to the study of the members of the house in order that it may be discussed on second reading.

But I am not complaining about that, except to state that 1 was not present when this report was placed before the committee. If I had been,
I should have endeavoured to secure the insertion of a reference to certain matters w'hich I regard as important.
First, from sitting on that committee I found little by way of criticism of or reproach against the existing commission. I think the chairman of that commission, Mr. Charles-worth, is a gentleman of high culture, of literary experience and artistic taste, and a very useful member of a commission or board such as this. The impression I received was that he had not had experience in administering business affairs to the extent necessary to enable him to look carefully after the financial administration of the commission.
I heard nothing by way of evidence which cast any reproach upon Colonel Steel, who is regarded not only in this country but also in the neighbouring republic as one of the most eminent men connected with radio transmission work. I think if I had been present when the report was drawn up I would have suggested leaving out certain references to the political broadcasting. I admit that a certain script was placed before me of one broadcasting of the so-called Sage broadcast, which contained two references to the then leader of the opposition and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which I regard as uncalled for and tending toward defamation. There is no doubt in my mind, having been through it, that the investigation into a certain hydro electric power matter indicated that there had been an effort at organized corruption the like of which had never before been known in this country, and I should not have been surprised if, in making a political broadcast, either speakers on the platform or those who were preparing the script for a broadcast such as this should have made some reference to it. As a matter of fact I did not hear on any public platform any reference to the Beauharnois matter. I say further, while I am dealing with it, that I went through the evidence in the Beauharnois investigation and I heard what was said before the committee and what was said outside of the committee, and I did not hear of any evi-
Broadcasting Corporation

dence which cast any reflection upon the personal honour and integrity of the present Prime Minister, who then also was Prime Minister. That is clear in my mind, and I deprecate any such reference as was made in the Sage script.
But in dealing with defamation over the radio, hon. members know as well as I do that the practice was not confined to the propagandists of any one political party. There were sent to me examples which on their face appeared to be extreme defamation and which had been sponsored either by the Liberal party or by individual members of that party. I refrained from placing them before the committee because I thought that was not a proper matter for inquiry under the circumstances. For instance, one related to the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), with whom I have had grave differences of opinion on political matters relating to his retirement from the late government. Nevertheless it would be very difficult to justify to me the radio propaganda which was directed by the Liberal party against him and his personal reputation and personal conduct. I believe that such matters should be eliminated from political discussion at election time or otherwise. So I should like to have had just a little different reference in this respect to political broadcasts. But I do not think the personnel of the commission were shown to be responsible either for the defamation by Liberal propagandists or for the defamation by Conservative propagandists which came over the radio at certain times. I listened myself to certain addresses delivered in the province of Quebec by some of my political opponents, which caused me to smile with contempt, but I think if they were stenographically reported they could not but be deemed defamatory, and I believe that the commission, if continued as a commission, would certainly have taken these matters under their consideration, because prior to the general election, at the suggestion of the then government, a by-law was adopted by the commission prohibiting political propaganda of a defamatory character.
I do not think much is to be gained by the new legislation. All that was desirable could have been attained by a few slight amendments to the present statute and by the appointment of a business manager to deal exclusively with financial and business operations. It is perhaps not to be expected that Mr. Charlesworth would be thoroughly competent and qualified for the financial part of the work, but I think the work he and his associates have done since they were appointed, the difficulties they have overcome and the problems they have solved entitle them to high com-
mendation and praise from this parliament and from the public in general. After listening to the witnesses and having read the report I have a slight suspicion that perhaps there is rather a political aim to be served by this proposed bill than to have material and satisfactory remedies provided for the existing defects. However I am not going to oppose the measure but shall let it go through. Perhaps in the course of a year or two-

speechtext: As chairman of the special committee to inquire into radio broadcasting in Canada, it is perhaps proper that at this time I should offer a few remarks on this resolution. In the first place may I answer the criticism of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in connection with his absence from the meeting-

If the hon. gentleman will allow me to make my statement. The clerk of the committee put the notice into the -mail box of every member of the committee the evening prior to the final meeting to prepare the report and present it to the house, and if my hon. friend did not receive that notice it must be either that he did not go to his mail box or else the notice was mislaid by him. But even if he did not receive the notice, I, as chairman, made an effort to have the hon. member attend that meeting. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) was asked to try to locate the hon. member, but at the time we were not able to locate him. I am not making any criticism, but I want to make it clear that the members of the committee made every effort

Broadcasting Corporation
to have every member of that committee at that final meeting before our report was prepared for presentation to the house.
May I say that it was one of the great privileges which I have enjoyed since I have been in public life to be chairman of this committee. Hon. members from all parties showed me every courtesy, and made my work light, because they did most of it. I think the aim of every member of the committee was to try to improve radio broadcasting in Canada. There was no other object. At the same time, we had an order of reference from the House of Commons, which we were obliged to follow. We were instructed to do certain things. When my hon. friend criticizes the clause which relates to the Mr. Sage broadcasts, he had the same privilege as every other member of the committee; there was no limit to our investigation. Let me read one or two lines from the order of reference:
Also to inquire into the extent to which there has been any abuse of broadcasting privileges, either for political or advertising purposes, and to advise as to what principles should govern the regulations or control thereof.
So that we had to investigate any abuses concerning political broadcasting as we were ordered to do so. My hon. friend had the same privilege as any other member of the committee; if he knew of any abuses, political or otherwise, it was for him to bring them before the committee.
Now I wish to answer briefly one or two criticisms made by -the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). But before I do that may I say, Mr. Chairman, that the committee had before them the report of the Aird commission which made an extensive study of radio broadcasting in practically every country of the world and reported to the government of the day. We had also the evidence taken by the special committee in 1932, also the evidence taken by the special committee in 1934, and the evidence taken at the sittings of the committee this year. So that the committee, in arriving at their conclusions, had before them plenty of evidence on which they based the recommendations contained in the report, which recommendations, I am given to understand, will be embodied in a bill when this resolution is passed. Not only that, but this year we made an extensive inquiry. May I add that a great number of public bodies were anxious to make their presentations to the committee. They had made special studies of radio broadcasting not only in Canada but in all other countries. Not only did they appear
personally, but they prepared and presented to the committee extensive briefs. Representatives appeared in person in readiness to give members of the committee any explanation they might desire concerning the contents of the briefs presented. These bodies went to the trouble of preparing and presenting the briefs without any cost to the committee, and without pay for the work they had done. It is most gratifying to note that the people who appeared before us were prepared to do that. Their only object seemed to be that of giving better radio broadcasting in Canada.
As I stated previously we had before us the Aird report and the evidence taken in 1932 and 1934. Further, we had the recommendations made in 1934, which were not embodied in legislation. May I mention briefly the names of a few bodies which appeared before the committee. We had the Canadian Press, supported by Mr. J. F. B. Livesay, general manager, and Mr. E. Norman Smith, vice-president; Mr. Paul Coffey, representing the Young Men's Canadian Club; Mr. S. P. Dunlop, president of the Montreal Federation of Musicians, supported by Mr. W. M. Murdock, who represented the Canadian locals of the American Federation of Musicians; Mr. Alan B. Plaunt, honorary secretary of the Canadian Radio League, an organization composed of practical men throughout the dominion, men who have made a real study of radio broadcasting in Canada They had as their purpose giving Canada the best possible radio broadcasts under the circumstances. Then, we had Mr. Brooke Claxton, counsel for the Canadian Radio league, who appeared with Mr. Plaunt. We had the Reverend Father H. St. Denis, Professor of Philosophy at Ottawa university; Mr. Herbert Moore, of New York, president of the Transradio service, who lodged some charges against the Canadian Press. We had Mr. E. A. Weir, formerly with the Canadian radio commission; Mr. C. M. Pasmore of the MacLaren Advertising Company, Limited, Toronto; Mr. Glen Bannerman, of the Association of Canadian Advertisers; Mr. J. A. MacLaren, of the Canadian Association of Advertising Agencies; Mr. Harry Sedgwick, chairman of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters; Mr. W. T. Burford, representing the All Canadian Congress of Labour; Mr. R. W. Ashcroft, former general manager of the Trans-Canada Broadcasting Company; Hon. W. J. Major, Attorney General and Minister of Telephones and Telegraphs for the province of Manitoba, who also represented the telephone systems of the three
Broadcasting Corporation

western provinces. May I add that the publicly owned telephone system in Manitoba owns broadcasting station CKY, the most powerful station in Canada, and another one at Brandon. We had the Hon. J. L. Ralston, representing the Trans-Canada telephone system; Rev. H. L. Haslam, of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia.
In addition, many briefs were presented unaccompanied by witnesses. We received hundreds of letters containing requests, criticisms -of and praise for the radio commission. All those were placed before the committee. In presenting a concrete report I believe the committee should be commended. I do not believe the report of any special committee has received more favourable comment from the newspapers of Canada. I do not intend to weary this committee by quoting lengthy comments, although I have before me comments from newspapers of all political shades. They seem to agree that the unanimous report as presented to the house is satisfactory to Canadian listeners and to people generally who believe in a national broadcasting system in Canada. dence contained in the minutes of proceedings of the different meetings of the committee to prove that there was a lack of understanding and a lack of cooperation between the members of the commission. May I give just one example to make my point? And I am making no criticism of who got the contract or who did not. The radio commission entered into a contract for wire line network which involved an expenditure, under the contract, of $375,000, and which in the total aggregated an expenditure of $526,000. That contract was signed without the chairman of the commission knowing anything about it. Not only that, the contract was signed almost nine months before the contract which then existed expired. A few days after the contract was signed the chairman of the radio commission wrote a letter saying that it would be impossible to enter into a new contract as the one which already existed did not expire until April, 1936. If my right hon. friend were chairman of the commission and a contract were being entered into which involved that amount of expenditure, I am sure he would know what was in the contract before it was signed.
I am just about finished, Mr. Chairman, as I do not want to make any long speeches at this stage of the game. The committee refrained from making many specific recommendations because we wanted to leave the new body free in any administrative action they might take. However, the committee did make a specific recommendation with regard to future political broadcasting. I do not think there is any doubt but that the Canadian people were fed up with the broadcasting during the last election. There was too much broadcasting and I am sure the different parties spent money for broadcasting which could have been spent elsewhere to better advantage. The committee recommended that dramatized political broadcasts be prohibited. I think everyone is in favour of that recommendation, even the political parties that put out dramatized broadcasts during the last election.
Another recommendation was that full sponsorship of all political broadcasts be required. I think that is very necessary. Political broadcasts were put out during the last election without any sponsorship, and these broadcasts were sent out from the stations of the Canadian commission. I think every political broadcast should be sponsored by a party so that the people may know who is doing the broadcasting. There should not be any deception of the public. There is no doubt that during the last election certain dramatized broadcasts were sent out from the stations of the radio commissions with the

idea of deceiving the public into thinking they were dramatic productions. The public were deceived into listening to what they thought was drama, but which was nothing but a political broadcast. Another recommendation was:
That the limitation and distribution of time for political broadcasts be under the complete control of the corporation, whose duty it shall be to assign time on an equitable basis between all parties and rival candidates.
That no political broadcasts be allowed on an election day or during two days immediately preceding same.
Those are the only specific recommendations which were made. I want to thank the members of the committee who honoured me by making me chairman. If the bill which will follow this resolution embodies the main recommendations of this report, I believe radio broadcasting in Canada will be making progress, not only from the standpoint of the listeners but from the national standpoint.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps a word on the object in addition to what was said in the budget address is in order at this stage, and I shall admit at the outset that this is a very complicated matter which calls for considerably more legal knowledge than I have.
I can say at once that the object is to produce more revenue from the class of companies embraced within the next few sections. It is estimated, as closely as the officials can estimate it, that approximately 81,000,000 of additional revenue should be involved in the changes provided. The object is partly to reverse the taxation instituted, I believe, in 1933 whereby dividends paid out by certain companies were taxable, thus differing in principle from income tax in general, which is a tax upon income coming in. At that time there were difficulties which I can appreciate, difficulties in the form of surpluses accumulated prior to the time the taxation of 1933 came into force. These difficulties still exist, because many of these companies do not pay out their surpluses in the form of dividends but allow them to accumulate. It is thought better to inaugurate taxation based upon income rather than to rely upon being able, at some unknown date in the future, to tax, as provided for in the existing law, the disbursement of surplus. Surpluses tend to accumulate year by year, in many cases reaching very substantial sums, and there is at least some difficulty when we contemplate the possibility of such companies being able to get out at some stage without paying a tax upon their disbursements in the form of dividends. I shall not attempt to discuss the legal possibilities in that regard. It will perhaps be sufficient at this stage to say that it must be remembered that some of these corporations have no assets in Canada, nothing which can be attached here, and the sums involved are considerable. For that reason the government is of the view that it would be far better to tax the revenue of such companies as it comes in rather than to rely upon receiving taxation from them as they pay out that revenue, now or in the future, in the form of dividends.
It may be asked: Why halve the normal corporation tax rate? The present rate of taxation on some companies, in so far as they are taxed under the present law, is 5 per cent when they pay out their dividends. As to making the tax half the normal corporation rate, the reason is, of course, as I indicated in committee of ways and means, our desire not to drive these corporations out but to make them pay revenue to the dominion treasury. Obviously, if we taxed them too highly from their own point of view, being international they could move anywhere and they would undoubtedly move out. I am of the opinion that if we attempted to oharge the normal Canadian corporation tax all such companies would vanish from our midst and consequently be non-taxable. Indeed, representations are made to me that the rate of taxation proposed in the bill will have the effect of driving some of them elsewhere. Be that as it may, after listening to all the representations on the subject, we believe that this is fair taxation and should not involve the companies in question moving out, but should result in a substantial increase in revenue to the federal treasury from this source.

I think the minister
must be in error in assuming that such companies have no assets in this country that we can get control of, for this is the definition on page 2 of the bill:
"N on-resident-owned-investment corporation" means a company incorporated in Canada, at least ninety-five per centum of the aggregate value of whose issued shares and all of whose bonds, debentures and other securities or evidences of funded indebtedness are beneficially owned by persons who are nonresidents of Canada or are owned or held by trustees for the benefit of non-resident persons____

(i)	from the ownership of or the trading or dealing in bonds, stocks or shares, debentures, mortgages, hypothecs, bills, notes or other similar property, or any interest therein;

Obviously the corporation has assets in Canada, and obviously the assets arise from the fact that it is domiciled in Canada, because it must be incorporated in Canada.

Provided that there has been paid in respect of the income earned between the 1932 fiscal period and the fiscal period first taxed by reason of election under subsection 4 of section 9 of this act, or in respect of dividends equal in amount to the said income, an amount of tax equal, in the aggregate, to 5 per centum of the said income.	.
So long as we get five per cent of what is earned by w'ay of income during that period, that is all that matters.

That is not quite the general principle which has governed in connection with these taxing acts. We take the sum total of the income instead of computing it for the separate years. As the law now stands, we should be entitled to say: Your income in 1933 was 8100,000; we were then entitled to $5,000, and as you did not pay it we are entitled to interest for a period of two or three years,
As the law stands we are not entitled to anything until the income is paid out by way of dividends.

But we are predicating it on that assumption. As a matter of fact, they kept the money back from us; it was a scheme they devised for the purpose of escaping taxation. Then we say we shall take five per cent from that starting point in 1932 up to the date of election being made under this section subsequent to the coming into force of the section of the law which provides for the election. It is a nice question whether "said income" covers the aggregate.

tax on 2(p) companies with the dividend tax on 4(k) companies. It was felt desirable to transform this from a dividend tax into an income tax, and it is clear that if you raised it to 7J per cent there would not be the election which we desire to bring about.

As I understand it, what the minister says is this: Arbitrarily we have said that, in order to adjust upon a basis of equity the relations between these two classes of companies, payment shall be made of the tax upon two-thirds of the aggregate dividend received by that class of company from Canadian companies. That is the story.

As I understand the situation, the effort is, not to increase the toll taken from these companies, but to take it in a different form, because, they not having received the dividend we could not obtain it, but by taking it from income we receive it in a different form; and two-thirds of the dividend shall be treated as the whole dividend for the purpose of computing five per cent. Is that the story?

speechtext: That is the story, yes, very clearly put.

Section agreed to.
On section 13-Transfers in trust.

Are there any changes
in this? The law at present is very clear; I cannot in my lifetime create a trust which permits the corpus of the trust to come back to me, and thus avoid taxation. That is the general rule. Now what does this effect?
(3) Where a person transfers property in trust and provides that the corpus of the trust shall revert either to the donor or to such persons as he might determine at a future date or where a trust provides that during the life-time of the donor no disposition or other dealing with the trust property shall be made without the consent, written
or otherwise, of the donor, such person shall nevertheless be liable to be taxed on the income derived from the property transferred in trust or from property substituted therefor as if such transfer had not been made, unless the minister is satisfied that the contingencies expressed in the trust deed do not substantially affect what is in substance a bona fide gift and are not for the purpose of evading taxes on income imposed under this act.
The last part of that is new, is it not? As a matter of fact it does not need to be there at all as far as the law is concerned. Where a donor creates a trust and that trust leaves the corpus in his hands or subject to his disposition he still must pay taxes upon the income from it, because he has not effectually put it out of his control. This is to declare the law, I take it, in order that there may be no doubt about it. But the provision at the end I certainly do not think is desirable. It is very undesirable to say that the minister shall be satisfied about any contingency.
I think the officers of the department will say that the law has been thus administered. I have in mind a case in which a gentleman told me that he had undertaken to make a trust, but he discovered that he had endeavoured to maintain control over the disposition of the corpus and he was informed that the revenue from that must be taxable. In other words, to use the language of Lord Eldon that I have so frequently quoted, you cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time. \ou cannot say: It is my property now for my purposes, and belong to the trustee for another purpose. I do not like this idea of: -unless the minister is satisfied that the contingencies expressed in the trust deed do not substantially affect what is in substance a bona fide gift and are not for the purpose of evading taxes.
I submit that that is very unsound. If it is a gift, it is a gift; if it is a trust, it is a trust. The minister should not be the one to decide whether or not the donor has correctly interpreted his own intentions.

I am afraid I cannot argue
that point exhaustively. As I understand it, there are certain transactions described in the early part of the section which are not necessarily regarded as non-gifts, that is, are not necessarily transactions which leave the subject matter of the transaction in the hands of the donor. Let me read the subsection:
Where a person transfers property in trust and provides that the corpus of the trust shall revert either to the donor or to such persons as he might determine at a future date-

We are familiar with
that form of trust.

That would not be allowed
as a gift.

No; I think that is quite clear.
-or where a trust provides that during the lifetime of the donor no disposition or other dealing with the trust property shall be made without the consent, written or otherwise, of the donor-
That is no gift, because he still retains the power of disposition.
-such person shall nevertheless be liable to be taxed on the income derived from the property transferred in trust or from property substituted therefor as if such transfer had not been made

I wish the minister would stop there. It cannot be a bona fide gift and a trust fund at the same time. I think if the minister strikes these words out he will find it will not be an invitation to those who have to administer the act to depart from what is the declared sense of the law. I just suggest it.
Perhaps we could leave this section for the moment, and I shall be prepared to say a word about it a little later.

Yes. Have I made the point clear? As the minister has read the subsection, it is quite clear that it is divided into two classes. Neither can be called a gift. It is also clear that where the donor retains the powers of disposition, either directly or by reversion to him of the corpus, or to a person named by him, then he does not escape taxation. Why? Because the power of disposition remains with him. I think the minister is inviting trouble if he puts himself into the position where he can say: Oh, yes, it is true this was a trust deed, and all that sort of thing, but you want me to find that this is a bona fide gift. If it is a gift, there is never any trouble about realizing that it is not a trust, and the man knew it was not a trust when he started. This subjects the minister to pressure which should not be put upon him; it is unfair to him and to the administration of the legislation. I am trying to put myself in the minister's place;
I would not want to be subject to that form of pressure, having people come to me and say: It is true it is a trust, but I want you to say it is all right.

speechtext:
Section 15 clarifies the
matter.

If we were not to leave the word "only" in the section, we would be in a bad way. By this measure we provide for the payment of two instalments, and by section 14 we would be providing for the payment of four instalments.

The minister could have answered by saying that it is not intended that section 14 shall apply other than this year. I was simply asking whether the word "only" was used inadvertently, because clearly five per cent is to be the rate hereafter, and three per cent the penalty. It is not necessary to put in the word "only." But the minister has said that this is a separate thing standing by itself, and that therefore the word "only" should be there.
As regards section 15 is it desirable in these days of slow recovery to accelerate in that way the payment of income tax? Frankly, my observations would lead me to believe that with provincial taxes in most of the provinces the burden has become rather onerous, and to make instalments payable three in this year, and two in following years, is going to impose a heavy burden on a great many people.

On section 19-Exemption from gift tax.

Is it correct that this applies only to gifts of capital? It cannot apply to gifts of any kind, because a man pays his tax on his income. If I give away a thousand dollars surely I cannot have a gift tax on it.
