speechtext: The present gift tax applies to gifts whether they come from capital or income.
The tax is bad enough as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the way in which it has been administered so far; regardless of source, from either capital or income, it has so far been taxed. To some extent this is a relaxation.

I was told not. A man pays his tax at a certain rate, and he gives away a thousand dollars for some deserving purpose, possibly not to a charity, but for educational purposes; surely that should not be taxed. That would be absurd. The purpose of the act when it was put on the statute books was to prevent the distribution of capital under the guise of gifts, but the law was never meant to interfere with income; a man can do what he likes with his income after he pays his tax. No person ever thought of imposing a tax on the gifts a man made out of his income.

His freedom from all taxes on that does not depend upon whether it is taken out of his income; it depends upon whether it comes within the exemptions set out in the act.
Income War Tax Act
The exemptions do not touch it.
We have added another one. The exemptions are in section 88 of the act. I do not know that I need read them all. If he made a gift of one thousand dollars it would be exempt under this section.

I mean outside exemptions, altogether. I never have heard it suggested until this minute that it covered gifts made out of income, which had1 paid a high tax. Nobody ever thought of doing it until this minute. Look at the absurdity of it. I speak feelingly about it. You pay a thousand dollars to some youngster who is trying to get through university. You have already paid on that amount your income tax of, let us say for the sake of argument, at least thirty per cent, and now somebody says that you must pay a gift tax as well on that thousand dollars. The whole purpose of the gift tax was to meet the situation created by the distribution of capital by those who were endeavouring to escape taxation by making family gifts, as was the case in the United States. But in the United States they never thought of imposing a tax on gifts made out of income. I have made inquiries about the matter, and if this is to be the law, it will necessitate revision of my taxation account, at any rate. I have never heard of anything of the sort, and certainly as far as I know it has never been so interpreted in this country. It would be absurd if it were so, and the sooner it is ended the better. Every time I give away a quarter on the street to a chap to get something to eat, do I have to keep an account of that- because I give it out of my income, on which I have already paid income tax amounting to from thirty to fifty per cent? The reason for the gift tax was so clear. I remember when the gift tax was brought down by the minister. We followed the course that had been taken by the United States where fortunes were being distributed to escape taxation by the donor dividing his fortune among his family before death. There were three events that were challenged by the taxing authority. There was, first, the creation of a trust. If the trust completely severed1 the donor from his property, it was not taxable. If the donor still retained disposition of the corpus, it was taxable. People got over that by making outright gifts of $100,000 or $200,000 or $300,000, and that transferred the property and ended the matter. We followed, for the purpose of dealing with that very situation. The minister had in mind a particular case

which had arisen. Suppose I gave S100 to the Red Cross; that is a charity and therefore is exempt from taxation. But suppose I give $100 to someone I have never seen, who desires to complete his education in Saskatchewan. Must I pay, in addition to the tax I have paid on that as part of my income, a gift tax as well?
Surely not in addition.

That is the situation
exactly. That is the absurdity of it.
Mi-. NEILL:	Is it not rather that you
are not allowed to deduct that; you cannot claim it as an exemption?
No. They want me to pay a gift tax on it in addition.

The commissioner of income tax advises me that no inquiry is made as to whether the gift is made out of income or principal, and in all the cases put by the right hon. gentleman he would be exempt because the gifts he enumerated are among the exemptions.
No.
The thousand dollars-

No; the thousand dollars has long since gone, and so has the payment to charity. They tax the gifts made out of my income. The authorities have advised me that gifts for education and matters of that kind cannot be taxed.
There is an exemption.

But it is a limited exemption. I am talking of sums that far exceed the exemption. Surely it is not suggested in this country that, after having paid the present high rates of income taxes, if you give away money for any purpose in the world that is not covered by section 88, you have to pay a gift tax when the money comes out of your income.
It is ridiculous.
Not only ridiculous, but the statute never meant that.

Surely that was not ever intended to be the law of Canada. It certainly was not the intention of the former minister when he introduced the tax, or of parliament when it passed it. I recall vividly the circumstances that gave rise to its coming into operation. What is more, this will mean that people will have to revise their whole accounting arrangements because everybody is giving away money from time to time, I hope, to the extent of his ability, and he never thinks, because he gives it out of his income, therefore it is subject to a gift tax. suggested this to me before. It seems so absurd. Where a man has a large fortune and gives away $100,000 to this member of his family, $100,000 to another, and so on* to escape taxation-that is what the statute was passed for. I do not want to talk about my own affairs, but during the last year I have helped in education in every province of this dominion, I have aided young people, some of whom I have never seen, and as long as the money came out of my income I did not think it was taxable; neither did the former minister who brought in the gift tax. I do not think that was ever intended.
I believe it was not intended, and I think the section should be corrected. But that is the way it reads.

Surely the minister will not say that there has ever been anyone who has paid a gift tax on a gift made out of income. Certainly I never heard of such a thing until I heard it in this committee tonight. Money taken out of the income of a man who has paid his income tax and surtax is now to be taxed. They could not possibly have known of it; the agent could not have retained the amount out of his remittances, and he will simply have to make it up in some way out of his own resources, which would not be fair. For instance, companies in the old country or in Germany or France, or wherever they may happen to be, certainly will not now pay a retroactive tax, and I earnestly suggest to the minister that in cases of that kind the tax should not be made applicable until the date it was announced, May 1.

There are always objections to retroactive taxation, but it has been the practice here, ever since there have been
amendments to the Income War Tax Act, to make the amendments, many of them at least, retroactive to the extent of the previous year. I do not think, therefore, that any more injustice will be done in this case than in the case of ordinary individuals. The view we have taken is that the five per cent is taxable on the whole remittance as the law stood. This now says that the five per cent is applicable only to forty per cent of the remittance. The companies claim that we should come to their point of view as regards last year and say that they should pay only five per cent on ten per cent of the remittance. We never concurred in their view that only ten per cent should be taxed. They want us not only to agree that that was the law but to confirm it now for last year. We have considered the matter and do not think we should do so.

While it is true that we have made the income tax retroactive or applied it to last year, that is quite normal because income tax returns for last year's income as a rule are not made until early this year. All I am asking in this case-I am not criticizing the rate of taxation proposed; I accept that-is that this tax, which is in the nature of a duty, should not be made applicable until the date the tax was announced, because the poor agent in this country, as far as I can see, is the one who will have to pay the tax. He having had a contract, and having fulfilled his contract and made his remittances, his company or his principals certainly would not think of returning to him the taxes for last year which now suddenly and unexpectedly become payable. I think the agent is the one who will have to bear the weight of this taxation. This is not something that is sweeping over a very wide field and for the future we could make clear what is taxable and impose the taxation, but in justice, fairness and equity to the agent I submit that the tax should not be applicable this year prior to May 1, the date when the budget came down.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one word on section 89, which is a new section being added to the act by section 20 of this bill. I had intended to say something but we passed the section fairly quickly. Would it not be desirable to provide that the regulations shall be printed in the gazette? This is an extraordinary power which is being left to one man, and in view of the declared general policies of the administration I think it might be desirable that the regulations should be published in the gazette, and that notice should be given when the certificate issues. I do not wish to prolong the discussion in committee, but certainly in view of that power which is given, I think it would be desirable from the public standpoint, and from the standpoint of the minister himself, to have the regulations published in the gazette, and notice given when the certificate issues. Under the old law relating to the Interior department, when certain lands were alienated a certificate to that effect was issued, and I think a great deal of improvement may be effected in connection with the administration of the law if publicity is given as I suggest.
Notice to whom?
Notice to the world in the gazette-notice is hereby given.
I think publication in the gazette is reasonable, but I am just wondering whether it would not be sufficient if I gave an undertaking that notice will be published in the gazette.

The kind of notice I had reference to was such as was usually given under the Department of the Interior Act. For instance, under subsection 3 of section 89 you would say: Notice is hereby given that on July 1, 1937, a certificate was issued by the
minister that a mine known as

was
deemed to have come into production from and after that date. That is what I mean. It is the old provision that had to do with publication in connection with any alienation of the public domain. In this case it is a question of lessening public taxation.

I do not see that anybody is legitimately interested in that notice except the company. The public is likely to be misled by such a notice. I see no reason for publicity; on the other hand there are many objections against it. Speculators would say: The government has given a certificate that this mine has come into production. Now we do not know whether or not the mine is any good, but for our purposes we have come to
(Mr. Usley.]
the conclusion that it has come into production. That fact should not be paraded round the country as an invitation to persons to put their money into that mine; yet that is what might happen. I do not see what good it would do. The people interested in the notice are the people who will get the exemption, and we will tell them.

I would think it is far wider than that, but I shall not undertake to discuss it to-night. In any event the minister has to issue a certificate; I can move in the House of Commons to have it tabled, and therefore it follows that ultimately it may become a public document. I was suggesting that we follow the course which was pursued under our statutes in the early days with respect to the alienation of the public domain, when a certificate was published in the gazette with respect to lands in western Canada, mines, timber limits and matters of that sort. The gazette may not be the best place in the world to do it. But if any man has the duty cast upon him under the law, I submit that it is in the public interest that he discharge that duty involving the issuing of a certificate itself and publishing it in the gazette of the country, to the effect that notice is given; that pursuant to the provisions of section so-and-so a certificate has been issued that the mine has come into production. If the minister does not think well of the suggestion, I am quite content, but I think something of that sort would be in the interest of the minister as well as of the country.

I may say that following that inquiry I secured information which I think will provide what the leader of the opposition had in mind. The facts of the matter are that Major Barnett was appointed to represent the Department of Finance in Saskatchewan in connection with the moneys advanced for relief in the drought area. That is to say, his duties related specifically to the accountable advance of $9,000,000 which was made for relief in the drought area. Major Barnett was appointed in November, 1934. Subsequently Mr. Burgess, whose name was also mentioned in the previous discussion, and certain other clerks were engaged to assist Major Barnett. When Major Barnett resigned, Mr. Burgess took his place in May, 1935. There was some trouble between the dominion government and the Saskatchewan government as to payments under the farm placement scheme, and there was a short period during which Major Barnett, acting for the dominion government, did assume responsibility for payments under the farm placement scheme. However, distribution was actually made from lists supplied by the province of Saskatchewan, the certificates of expenditure being signed by Major Barnett and countersigned by Mr. Symons, the resident auditor of the Department of Labour who has been in the service of the department since he was seconded from the income tax branch in November, 1931. While Major Barnett did supervise these expenditures during that brief period, there was no report made by him on the farm placement scheme in Saskatchewan. My right hon. friend will recall that that was one of the main points of his inquiry. speechtext: On Friday evening the hon. member asked me if I was prepared to give a statement as to the number of those on relief in April of this year as compared with April of last year, or at any rate to give some comparison between the numbers on relief this year and last year. I may say that we now have available the preliminary figures for May of this year which can be compared with the figures for May of last year. .The preliminary figures for May of this year indicate that there are 261,674 heads of families on relief, which figure includes 25,572 heads of families in the drought areas of the prairie provinces. Exclusive of the dried out areas the dependents and individual cases numbei 878,908. In the dried out areas there are 104,379 dependents and individual cases, and the total number on direct relief for the month of May is, therefore, 1,244,961 as compared with 1,277,464 in May, 1935, a reduction of 2-54 per cent. In addition, in May, 1936, there were 19,596 single homeless persons cared for as compared with 37,024 in May, 1935, a reduction of 47-07 per cent. There were employed on relief works at wages during May, 1936, 5,991 persons as compared with 12,330 in May, 1935, a reduction of 51-41 per cent. The number of persons placed under this plan, by the nature of the plan, will be larger with each succeeding year. These figures represent, I believe, the proportions of the relief iproblem at the present time as compared with last year, and obviously we have to consider the problem in a relative sense, using the figures of the preceding years as a measure of increase or decrease under the particular categories which I have given the committee. speechtext:
According to this legislation the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will be bound to give a certain guarantee. I ask him one thing on behalf of the country; it is, not to practise any illegal operation on the east block for the removal of the viscera of the office of the Prime Minister into another building. It is not possible, according to the numerous returns which have been tabled at the very table before which the minister sits, to get any information about the matter. I will not insist on it any more at this time, but I have a lot to say, and I will say it elsewhere.
I have one thing to say in conclusion. It is, that all that has been done has not been done in vain, because that loan was mentioned in this committee on April 27 of this year, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which prior to that time had paid only $12,000,000 on the capital of the loan, decided to pay, three days after that speech, on May 1, the total amount, both capital and interest, which was due. If what has been said did not serve any other purpose, it served at least to force the refunding of that loan.
I hope that one document which is a state paper just as much as any paper can be, the guarantee of $60,000,000 on behalf of the dominion government, will, either as an exact copy or a carbon copy, remain on file. Why do we not have it now? It is because the then Prime Minister did not mind his own business, and was acting on behalf of all his ministers. In fact the few letters that were signed by the then Minister of Finance are still there, but they were signed after the order in council was passed, late in the fall. Therefore, sir, to be practical, I am sure that every minister will make a distinction between confidential and state papers. I had so much trouble, during the five years when the late government was in power, in getting some correspondence. I was told always that it was confidential. Here we have state papers which are therefore official and public, and they have vanished; it is impossible to get any trace of them. In England the thing would be decided by a court. In Canada we are more lenient. I cannot understand how such papers could have disappeared. It is impossible to find a trace of this document to which I refer, and the only copy which is on record in the Prime Minister's office is not a carbon copy of that famous and unforgettable letter; it is a copy of a return which has been tabled in this house.
3748	COMMONS
Unemployment-Relief Expenditures
Sir, the soil has been scratched. I attribute motives to no one, but I find it shameful to think that state papers which belong to this country have vanished. I cannot explain that, but the returns say so; the returns are official, and they will not disappear, because they will be locked in a room set apart for that purpose in the House of Commons. But the other papers belong just as much to the country. That is why I protest so strongly against their disappearance.

No, Mr. Chairman. In view of the observations that have been made by the hon. member (Mr. Pouliot) who has just taken his seat, I think it is very desirable to refer briefly to the matters to which he has alluded. It will be within the memory of this committee that the House of Commons standing committee heard witnesses with respect to this guarantee of S60,000,000 by the government of Canada. Departing from the general rule, I attended that committee, and I offered to be sworn, telling Colonel Ralston that if he desired to swear me I would be sworn. I gave my evidence, as did all witnesses before that committee, without being sworn, and on that occasion there were produced all the documents which had to do with this transaction. The letter to which reference has been made would naturally be in the hands of the addressee; that is where one would expect to find it. A copy of it was printed1 in the report which I have in my hands. Together with all the communications that passed, it will be found in the report of the banking and commerce committee. The Canadian Pacific Railway company paid S12.000.000 of the obligations, and this year retired the balance of it, $36,000,000, and the arrangement, that is the underwriting, was made, obviously, long before the matter was mentioned in this house. The guarantee was for a period of five years. I believe three of the years had expired when the payments were made in full. It was explained before the committee, not only by myself but by the president of the company, that the reason the order in council was not passed until the fall was because the president went to England hoping that he would be able to secure consent from the British authorities to sell his debenture stock upon the markets there. That permission was not forthcoming. On my return the order in council was prepared, and it has been frequently presented, in answer to a return of this house, and in the report of the committee on banking and commerce. I may add that the various letters which passed between Mr. Dodds and Sir George Perley are 
set out in this report of the committee on banking and commerce, from March 6, 1934 to June 14, 1934. In view of what has been said, since the member has made charges of illegality and wrongdoing and matters of that kind, I desire, in fairness to my colleagues as well as myself, to make a few observations, which I shall do at a later time, when we have again convened.
